articles.title: Trump leans into trolling critics as GOP midterm anxiety grows
articles.summary: President Trump is leaning into online trolling, off-color attacks and picking fights over geographical names as his approval rating sinks just weeks out from November’s midterm elections. Over the weekend, Trump raised eyebrows when he floated changing the name of New Mexico to “New America” weeks after he swapped the name of Lake Ontario to…
articles.body:
President Trump is leaning into online trolling, off-color attacks and picking fights over geographical names as his approval rating sinks just weeks out from November’s midterm elections.

Over the weekend, Trump raised eyebrows when he floated changing the name of New Mexico to “New America” weeks after he swapped the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” amid the ongoing trade war with Canada. Trump also posted an image of the U.S. flag covering all of North America, the Caribbean, Greenland and Iceland. The move resulted in Iceland summoning the U.S. ambassador.

Additionally, Trump also stoked chatter when he posted to social media an AI video of him as the Green Lantern in an effort to tout his administration’s agenda.

Outrage has also grown against another animated video in which he is shown beating Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney with a hockey stick. The video was not posted by Trump but by an account supporting the president.

Democrats used some of the online posts to underline the contrast with Republicans, accusing Trump of not being focused on key issues.

“Under Democratic leadership here in New Mexico, we’re providing families with free childcare and college, protecting access to health care and investing in housing. While the White House wastes time coloring on maps, Nuevo México is busy doing the work,” New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham (D) said in a statement.

Former Rep. Charlie Dent (R-Pa.) said Trump’s posts referencing New Mexico as “New America” only serve to hurt Republicans running in the midterms.

“It’s hurting his own team. It’s almost like there’s an intentional act to undermine your own party’s prospects in the midterms,” Dent said in an interview with MS NOW’s Peter Alexander.

On top of facing historical headwinds, Republicans are grappling with the fallout over the U.S. war in Iran, which has led to higher energy prices and inflation.

Republicans argue Trump’s posts are all part of a strategy meant to galvanize the president’s base as the party faces historical headwinds and low approval ratings going into November.

“The issue isn’t his trolling, it is what it means. He is not crazy. He’s doing this on purpose: He thinks it motivates his base. And he is usually right about that. Or at least, the party has to trust him on that,” one former Trump administration official told The Hill.

The focus on base turnout has echoed throughout the GOP ecosystem this cycle. Republicans argue that Trump is their best turnout mechanism for the base, and that the party apparatus will handle targeting persuadable voters.

“We need him to think his name is on the ballot,” said Dan Eberhart, a Republican donor. “The worst thing for Republicans is a disengaged Trump.”

Trump asked his base to actually “pretend” that he is on the ballot in November, warning his agenda will get blocked by a Democratic majority.

“That’s the plan. And with the war unlikely to end and gas prices unlikely to come down, it probably isn’t the worst plan they could come up with,” the former official said.

However, other Republicans say Trump’s online trolling will have no impact whatsoever on voters, noting the posts and memes are mostly consumed by an online and Beltway-centric audience.

“At the end of the day, what he does on social media or even how it’s reported on cable news isn’t really what’s going to move voters one way or another,” said one Republican strategist.

“Do I think it shows he’s not focused on what matters? Yes. Do I think he’s doing it to motivate his base? I don’t know. But in either direction, I don’t think it matters,” the strategist added. “It’s going to come down to how people feel overall [about] how the economy is doing, and is he and the admin truly focused on it.”

“On that front, I wouldn’t feel great about it if I was a Republican consultant responsible for keeping a Senate majority and certainly a House majority,” the strategist said.

Polls show a majority of Americans are unhappy with the administration’s handling of the economy. According to a poll released by the Financial Times and Focaldata on Tuesday, Trump’s approval sat at 33 percent among registered voters. The same poll also showed that 66 percent said they believed the economy was going in the wrong direction.

When asked about the criticisms of Trump’s online posts, the White House said he “can walk and chew gum at the same time.”

“As the leader of the free world, he’s well equipped to stand up for America’s national interests on the world stage while working to lower costs here at home,” said Allison Schuster, a White House spokesperson.

The unnamed Republican strategist said the posts from Trump’s social media account could provide a glimpse into what will be heard from the president and his allies at this week’s midterm convention in Dallas and the campaign trail leading up to November.

“They’re just wholly misguided by that because even the president’s base, the people that turned out and propelled him to victory — whether they were traditional MAGA voters or even Hispanic voters — if they are undecided both in the elections or even to show up and vote, they’re not going to base it on anything other than how they’re feeling about the economy,” the strategist said.

articles.title: Conflicting court rulings leave Missouri’s congressional map in limbo
articles.summary: Republicans rushed to the high court after the Missouri Supreme Court ruled the state could not use the redrawn map, which was designed to eliminate one Democratic-held seat, this year.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — A fast-moving fight over whether Missouri Republicans can use a redrawn congressional map for this fall’s midterm elections was cast into chaos on Tuesday with two different courts issuing conflicting rulings. In one, the U.S. Supreme Court, in an order issued by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, left in place a Missouri Supreme Court ruling from last week that said the map could not be used while a ballot initiative that could lead to voters rejecting the newly drawn district lines moves forward. Kavanaugh handles emergency requests that arise from Missouri. But soon after, a federal judge in Missouri ruled in favor of two GOP congressional candidates who argue that the new map, which was in place for the August primaries, must be used in November in order to avoid federal constitutional violations. That case could also quickly face U.S. Supreme Court scrutiny with time running out for the map to be finalized. The state’s deadline to finalize ballots was 5 p.m local time, and first ballots are set to go out Sept. 19. Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe and Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, both Republicans, said on X Tuesday evening that the redrawn map would be used for the November election. The two cases raise different legal issues, with the Missouri Supreme Court focused only on state law while the federal case raises questions under the U.S. Constitution. The 2025 Republican redistricting plan, part of a wave prompted by President Donald Trump, was designed to eliminate one of the state’s two Democratic-held seats, currently held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver. If the Missouri Supreme Court ruling remains in effect, a map drawn in 2022, with six Republican-held seats and two Democratic-held seats, would be in place for the general election. The new lawsuit was filed by Rick Brattin, the Republican nominee in the district currently held by Cleaver, as well as Rep. Bob Onder, R-Mo. and two voters. The legal clash erupted after the 2025 redistricting plan was enacted. A group called People Not Politicians Missouri, led by Richard von Glahn, gathered signatures in support of a state referendum that would veto the Legislature’s map and put it on hold for the 2026 election. But Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, refused to put the measure on the ballot, arguing that redistricting plans are not subject to being overturned by voters. The Missouri Supreme Court found that Hoskins should not have rejected the plan, unanimously concluding there is nothing in state law that says redistricting plans are exempt from the referendum process. The referendum petition was “legal, sufficient and timely,” the court found. Under state law, whenever a proposed ballot initiative that overrides the Legislature is deemed valid, the law is automatically put on hold until after the people vote on it. The court also said any confusion caused by its ruling was a result of Hoskins’ delay in deciding whether the referendum could move forward. Hoskins waited until the last minute to reject the proposal ahead of an Aug. 4 deadline and broke with the state’s typical process of putting a law facing a veto referendum on hold when enough signatures are submitted. In the separate federal case, U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark, ruled that the state must use the map that people voted in during the primary. Using the old map would violate the rights of candidates under the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause and the provision of the Constitution that outlines how members of the House are elected, he found. Hoskins argued at the Supreme Court that the state court ruling violated the U.S. Constitution’s elections clause, which he said delegates significant powers to state legislatures in overseeing elections. The Supreme Court rejected a similar argument in a redistricting case from North Carolina in 2023. Hoskins’ lawyers told the justices that the state court ruling had created chaos because the new map was used in this year’s primary election. If the state has to revert to the old map, “hundreds of thousands of Missourians will see their votes in the primary election rendered pointless,” they wrote. Lawyers for the referendum supporters said in court filings that Hoskins was seeking at the Supreme Court a “political victory to which he was never entitled under the Missouri Constitution.” In May, the Supreme Court rejected a similar attempt by Democrats in Virginia who sought to revive their own congressional map that had been approved by voters. The Virginia Supreme Court had found legal flaws in the process that led to the referendum.

articles.title: What to watch in New Hampshire tonight: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. Before polls close tonight in New Hampshire’s primaries, Bridget Bowman and Ben Kamisar preview the key races to watch. Plus, Natasha Korecki digs into how Republicans are reviving their anti-trans playbook ahead of November. — Adam Wollner Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here. New Hampshire primaries test Trump and the left By Bridget Bowman and Ben Kamisar President Donald Trump’s endorsement will be put to the test once again in New Hampshire’s primaries, where liberal Democrats are also looking to cap an ascendant primary season with additional victories. Here’s what to watch tonight: Democratic Senate primary: Rep. Chris Pappas, who first won a battleground seat in 2018, is considered the front-runner for his party’s nomination in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. He already appears to be gearing up for the general election, focusing his campaign on addressing high costs and political corruption, while launching an ad attacking a potential Republican opponent. But Pappas is facing a challenge from the left from Karishma Manzur, a scientist and a member of the Democratic Socialists of America who supports progressive policies like “Medicare for All.” Manzur has sharply criticized Pappas over support and funding for Israel, saying he is “enabling genocide.” (For more on this primary, check out the latest edition of Steve Kornacki’s “Data Dive” newsletter.) Republican Senate primary: This contest includes multiple candidates, but the race is largely between two former senators: John Sununu and Scott Brown. Sununu represented New Hampshire in the Senate from 2003 through 2008 after serving in the House. He lost his bid for re-election in 2008 to Shaheen, but Republicans believe his well-known family name could give him a boost: Sununu’s brother and father both served as governors. Sununu is backed by President Donald Trump, Senate Majority Leader John Thune and the National Republican Senatorial Committee. Brown held a Massachusetts seat for three years, previously ran for the New Hampshire Senate in 2014, and served as Trump’s ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa during the president’s first term. General election preview: Trump lost New Hampshire by just 3 points in 2024, giving Republicans hope about making this open-seat race competitive. The GOP has not won a Senate race there since 2010, but New Hampshire does have a Republican governor, Kelly Ayotte. Read more → 🗺️ Senate landscape: Eight weeks from Election Day, there’s an increasing sense in both parties that the Senate is up for grabs this fall, even in red territory, Bridget reports. Tune in to the Kornacki Cam at 7 p.m. ET to watch Steve break down tonight’s results. Republicans return to a familiar playbook in Texas Analysis by Natasha Korecki The first ad from Elon Musk’s super PAC in Texas’ competitive Senate race has arrived. And it centers on a go-to topic for Republicans: transgender issues. The Musk-funded America PAC just released an ad titled: “Non-binary.” It features Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico saying, “God is non-binary,” twice in 15 seconds. The spot also notes that Talarico did not support a bill to ban biological men from playing in women’s sports. As a bookend, Republican Ken Paxton’s campaign posted on social media this morning an AI-generated ad featuring similar messaging. With this and other similar ads in races in red-leaning states, Republicans are demonstrating that in their high-stakes endeavor to retain Senate control, they believe their best bet is to return to the well. Some political observers credited the ubiquitous ads President Donald Trump ran in the 2024 election — “Kamala is for they/them; President Trump is for you” — as an influential factor in tanking Kamala Harris’ campaign. But will they work two years later? Harris’ 2024 loss fueled intraparty soul-searching and feuds over whether it was an error to allow those attacks to go unanswered. Whether the Talarico campaign will directly respond to these anti-trans ads in the future remains unclear. Talarico has called his past comments “cringey” but said Paxton, Texas’ attorney general, was clipping them to “distract from his career of corruption.” Talarico has also criticized the media for focusing too heavily on trans athletes and not enough on affordability, and spent months saying that some politicians were attempting to pit rank-and-file voters against one another. “What I would say is that the only minority destroying this country is the billionaires,” Talarico said in 2025. “Trans people are 1% of the population. Undocumented people are 1% of the population. Muslims are 1% of the population. We are all focused on the wrong 1%. Trans people aren’t taking away our healthcare. Undocumented people aren’t defunding our schools. Muslims aren’t cutting taxes for themselves and their rich friends. It’s the billionaires and their puppet politicians.” The political climate in America has decidedly shifted since 2024. Democrats have demonstrated, including in Virginia and Nebraska, that anti-trans ads did little to move voters who cared more about cost of living issues. Poll after poll shows that in the run-up to the midterms, voters are frustrated by the cost of groceries and gas. An unpopular war in Iran drags on. Trump’s popularity is in free fall. Scores of Latino voters, a sizable voting bloc in Texas, are angry over aggressive immigration tactics, while Trump has lost significant ground on support on the issue. In Texas specifically, fury over data center expansion is in full force. And Republicans locally are facing backlash over the administration’s border construction in Big Bend National Park. That may be why, when asked today, Talarico’s campaign had nothing to say about the new anti-trans ads. Instead, it released an ad featuring an endorsement from the former Texas attorney general’s director of law enforcement, David Maxwell, who served as a whistleblower against Paxton in his impeachment trial. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Kavanaugh won’t revive Missouri’s GOP-friendly congressional map for midterms
articles.summary: Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh on Tuesday refused to lift a block on Missouri’s new congressional map, which was poised to give Republicans a pickup opportunity in November. Missouri Republicans hoped to return to the new 7-1 House map favoring them after the Show Me State’s top court ruled officials must revert to their its existing GOP-leaning 6-2 House map for…
articles.body:
Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh on Tuesday refused to lift a block on Missouri’s new congressional map , which was poised to give Republicans a pickup opportunity in November.

Missouri Republicans hoped to return to the new 7-1 House map favoring them after the Show Me State’s top court ruled officials must revert to their its existing GOP-leaning 6-2 House map for the midterm elections.

Kavanaugh, an appointee of President Trump, handles emergency matters arising from Missouri by default. His one-sentence order declining to intervene contained no explanation.

It appeared to be a setback for Republicans, who had hoped to dismantle and flip a Kansas City-area seat held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D).

But the battle experienced another twist, however, when a federal judge separately ruled on Tuesday that changing maps so late would “wreak havoc.”

That judge, in response to a lawsuit filed by Rep. Bob Onder (R-Mo.), has temporarily ordered officials to continue implementing the GOP-leaning 7-1 House map that Republicans are pushing for.

“Widespread voter confusion would inevitably follow,” wrote U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark, an appointee of President Trump.

The dueling litigation in the state and federal courts does not make it immediately clear which congressional map will ultimately be used in November and introduces complications in Missouri on who qualifies to run for the general election, creating headaches for election officials and candidates alike.

Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway (R) said the state will follow Clark’s directive to move forward with the GOP’s favored 7-1 design.

“We appreciate Judge Clark’s support of the rights of Missouri voters, and intend to comply with this federal ruling. We maintain that changing the congressional map in between the primary and general elections is simply not feasible and profoundly unjust to Missouri voters,” Hanaway said in a statement.

Missouri Republicans have increasingly made that argument with less than 60 days before the election. They’ve warned that reverting to the old 6-2 design injects chaos in the state’s election system.

It marks the latest chapter of the mid-decade redistricting war to have reached the Supreme Court. Trump and national Republicans have pressured GOP-led states to redraw their House maps ahead of November as the party braces for a challenging midterm environment.

The party is looking to create pickup opportunities to cushion any potential blows Republicans might receive in November.

Previously, the Supreme Court revived a GOP-friendly map in Texas that had been struck down as a racial gerrymander but declined to restore a map that Virginia Democrats passed to combat it.

Unlike Texas, state judges in both Virginia and Missouri declared the redistricting efforts in violation of procedural requirements in each state’s constitution. Lawmakers then tried to convince the Supreme Court their cases raised federal concerns.

In Missouri, Republicans appealed a unanimous ruling from the state’s top court that the state’s new congressional map would not immediately go into effect. Instead, the state’s high court ruled at the time that the coalition behind efforts to put the map to a referendum in November would be allowed to have its measure placed on the ballot, meaning the map would not go into effect unless voters approved it in the fall.

“The Missouri Supreme Court made the right call in this case and Justice Kavanaugh was right to deny Missouri’s attempt to avoid the ruling of its highest court,” said Abha Khanna, a partner at Elias Law Group, a Democratic-aligned law firm that represented the referendum organizer.

“The state constitution is clear that Missourians should get the final word on whether their congressional map can undergo an extreme mid-decade gerrymander at President Trump’s request, and now they will,” Khanna added. “This is a win for democracy and for the hundreds of thousands of Missourians who signed a petition to make sure they would have a chance to weigh in on the gerrymandered HB 1 map.”

Republicans are still poised to pick up House seats in states like Texas, Florida, Ohio, Louisiana, Alabama, Tennessee, and North Carolina where new maps were put in place ahead of the midterms. Democrats responded in kind and are set to notch wins in California and Utah.

articles.title: SCOTUS rejects Missouri GOP bid to use revised congressional map in midterms
articles.summary: SCOTUS rejects Missouri Republicans' emergency bid over congressional maps, with Justice Kavanaugh ruling without comment and leaving the GOP-backed map blocked for the midterms.
articles.body: Justice Brett Kavanaugh on Tuesday denied Missouri's emergency appeal without comment, leaving in place the Missouri Supreme Court's ruling blocking the state's revised Republican-backed congressional map from being used in November's general election. Kavanaugh acted alone and did not refer the application to the full Supreme Court. The decision means Missouri will conduct the general election using its 2022 congressional districts after the state high court ruled the newer map never legally took effect because a voter-backed referendum suspended the law before it could go into effect. Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway had asked the Supreme Court to intervene after the Missouri Supreme Court ruled last week that the state's revised congressional map could not be used in November, despite having been used during last month's primary election. The emergency appeal was directed to Kavanaugh because he oversees emergency applications arising from the Eighth Circuit. MISSOURI AG FILES PETITION ASKING SUPREME COURT TO REVIVE TRUMP-BACKED REDISTRICTING MAP The revised map, backed by President Donald Trump and Missouri Republicans, was designed to make Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver's Kansas City-area district more favorable to Republicans, with the goal of expanding the GOP's congressional delegation from 6-2 to 7-1. The Missouri Supreme Court ruled the referendum petition filed by opponents after lawmakers approved the new districts prevented the map from taking effect unless voters ultimately approve it. The court concluded the congressional map adopted after the 2020 census "remains in full force and effect for the November 2026 general election." Hanaway argued the state faced an unprecedented situation after administering its primary election under one set of congressional districts only to be ordered to use another for the general election. In its emergency filing, Missouri told the Supreme Court it now faced "the unprecedented scenario of being forced to apply a starkly different congressional map in the 2026 General Election." The state argued election officials were uncertain whether they could comply with the Missouri Supreme Court's order with voting scheduled to begin within days. MISSOURI HIGH COURT BLOCKS GOP-BACKED CONGRESSIONAL MAPS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS; TRUMP BLASTS 'RIDICULOUS' RULING "Only this Court can prevent Missouri from being forced to disenfranchise hundreds of thousands of voters; and only this Court can ensure that Missouri hosts a timely and lawful federal congressional election," the application said. Hanaway also called the Missouri Supreme Court's ruling "catastrophic." "We have just appealed yesterday's catastrophic ruling to the Supreme Court of the United States," she said after filing the emergency appeal. "We look forward to the Court's prompt review of this critical matter, as our ability to hold timely and lawful congressional elections hangs in the balance." Opponents urged the justices to reject the request, arguing there was no genuine emergency because Missouri officials created the timing problem themselves. GEORGIA REDISTRICTING BATTLE REVIVED AFTER APPEALS COURT OVERTURNS FEDERAL COURT DECISION In their response, they argued the state's Secretary of State waited until "the last possible day" to challenge the referendum after implementing the revised map during the congressional primary, hoping the courts would refuse to order a return to the previous districts so close to the general election. "The Emergency Application for Stay does not present a real emergency," they wrote. They also argued the Supreme Court should not "reward the Secretary's scheme to outsmart Missouri voters, Missouri law, and the Missouri Supreme Court" by allowing the state to use a map the state's highest court concluded "is not the law and has never been the law." articles.summary: Click in for more news from The Hill {beacon} Healthcare Healthcare The Big Story Federal court to hear arguments on abortion pill access A three-judge panel on the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans will hear arguments Wednesday in a case that could eventually restrict the nationwide distribution of the abortion…
articles.body:
Federal court to hear arguments on abortion pill access

A three-judge panel on the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans will hear arguments Wednesday in a case that could eventually restrict the nationwide distribution of the abortion drug mifepristone .

The state of Louisiana is targeting Biden-era changes made in response to the COVID-19 pandemic that loosened regulations allowing mifepristone to be prescribed through telehealth, in pharmacies and through the mail without an in-person visit to a provider.

Medication has become the most common method of abortion since Roe v. Wade was overturned in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, with much of that increase coming from telehealth prescriptions.

According to the Guttmacher Institute, a think tank that supports abortion access, about 91,000 abortions were provided last year via telehealth prescription of abortion medication sent by mail to states with bans — including more than 9,300 in Louisiana.

The Louisiana case has put the Trump administration in an awkward political bind : It won’t defend moves made by the Biden administration, but Attorney General Todd Blanche has not yet settled the lawsuit, much to the disappointment of conservatives who have been pressuring him.

Instead, the administration has been urging judges to pause lawsuits while the Food and Drug Administration conducts a safety review of mifepristone.

The backstory: Louisiana is arguing that the FDA’s permissive rules undercut its near-total abortion ban and were a violation of the state’s sovereignty. A district judge said the state had a strong case, but sided with the Trump administration and paused the suit.

Louisiana appealed, and the 5th Circuit in May ruled in favor of the state, temporarily blocking telehealth prescriptions of mifepristone nationwide. But after an appeal, the Supreme Court paused the ruling and sent the case back.

Ahead of oral arguments, legal experts and abortion rights advocates anticipated the 5th Circuit—considered one of the most conservative appeals courts in the country— would rule for Louisiana again. But the panel hearing the case is comprised of two judges appointed by Democratic presidents, so there’s a possibility of a different outcome.

What’s next: No matter what, or when the 5th Circuit rules, there won’t be any changes to mifepristone prescribing; the Supreme Court will have the final say in the case.

The high court’s stay remains in effect throughout the appeals court proceedings, as well as through the Supreme Court’s disposition of a future petition, if any party to the case seeks one.

The Louisiana case is one of three federal lawsuits that could affect telehealth access to mifepristone nationwide. The others are being considered in Missouri and Texas .

The Texas case, which seeks to roll back mifepristone’s approval completely, was paused by a federal judge on Aug. 31. The Missouri case is still being briefed.

articles.body:
Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico released a new advertisement with a former aide to his Republican rival , Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.

According to The Texas Tribune, David Maxwell spent close to 10 years as the Texas attorney general’s director of law enforcement . Six years ago, Paxton was reported to the FBI by Maxwell and other officials, who asserted that the attorney general inappropriately utilized his office for his friend and political donor’s advantage. Maxwell and the other officials were fired in the wake of reporting on Paxton.

Maxwell backs Talarico in the ad , released Monday, saying, “Ken Paxton ended my five-decade career because I blew the whistle on his corruption.”

“I am supporting James Talarico for the U.S. Senate,” he adds.

Democrats usually have an uphill battle in the Lone Star State , but Paxton comes with notable baggage. The Texas attorney general has been dogged by scandal, previously facing impeachment in the Texas state House on corruption charges before being acquitted in the Texas Senate.

A recent poll showed Talarico was leading Paxton in the Senate race, with 47 percent supporting the Democrat and 40 percent backing the Republican.

Talarico is also facing a favorable electoral environment as November’s general election draws closer, with Democrats leading Republicans on generic congressional ballots, President Trump’s slumping approval rating and the unpopular war in Iran stretching past the six-month mark recently.

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 38.8 percent Tuesday evening, while his disapproval rating was at 56.7 percent.

The Hill has reached out to Paxton’s campaign for comment.

articles.title: Supreme Court declines to intervene in New York religious vaccine exemption case
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to intervene in a lawsuit brought by a New York mother who wanted to send her child to kindergarten while a challenge over the state’s vaccine requirements continues to play out. The mother, identified only as Jane Doe, was seeking emergency relief from the high court to keep her…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to intervene in a lawsuit brought by a New York mother who wanted to send her child to kindergarten while a challenge over the state’s vaccine requirements continues to play out.

The mother, identified only as Jane Doe, was seeking emergency relief from the high court to keep her 5-year-old son enrolled in an Eastchester, N.Y., school as courts weigh whether the state can legally deny religious exemptions for unvaccinated students.

The justices issued a one-line order denying Doe’s application. They offered no explanation for the decision, as is common with rulings on the court’s emergency docket.

Justices Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch noted they would have granted it.

The mother has claimed that her Catholic faith precludes her from further vaccinating herself and her child, writing in a statement to the school in April that she believes it is a “genuine, serious sin.”

New York eliminated its religious exemption to school vaccination requirements during a 2019 measles outbreak but continues to recognize medical exemptions, which Doe’s attorneys have argued infringes on her constitutional rights to direct her child’s religious upbringing.

Attorneys also stated that Doe faced “imminent forced relocation” to Florida if the justices did not step in because the state “provides no school-attendance route for a religiously objecting unvaccinated child.”

“A merits decision months later cannot reconstruct the beginning of a five-year-old’s kindergarten year,” they wrote in the application .

State officials defended lawmakers’ decision to repeal the religious exemption, citing an overarching need to stop the spread of infectious diseases.

“That response was rational because vaccination is widely recognized as an effective tool in promoting public health and preventing the severe harms that may result from vaccine preventable diseases,” a response brief signed by New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) stated. “And that response was narrowly tailored to address the precise cause of the recent decrease in immunization rates that threatened herd immunity in certain communities.”

Vaccination rates among kindergarteners are falling across the U.S., according to recently released data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), while exemptions are on the rise.

The data showed that 4.2 percent of American kindergarteners were exempted from one or more vaccines in the 2025-2026 school year, a slight uptick from the previous year.

The Department of Health and Human Services has made sweeping changes to vaccine policy during the second Trump administration, including lowering the number of recommended shots for children.

articles.title: Mamdani: NYC leaders ‘lied’ about post-9/11 air quality
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) on Tuesday released records related to the city government’s response to worsened air quality after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, saying city leaders “lied” about how safe it was to breathe. Mamdani’s office released 170,000 pages of records, with the mayor’s fiscal 2027 budget including $34 million…
articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) on Tuesday released records related to the city government’s response to worsened air quality after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, saying city leaders “lied” about how safe it was to breathe.

Mamdani’s office released 170,000 pages of records, with the mayor’s fiscal 2027 budget including $34 million to “create and maintain” a portal where the public can access those documents, according to a release .

“Close to 25 years later, more people have died from 9/11-related illnesses than were killed on the day itself,” Mamdani said at a press conference alongside family members of those who died on Sept. 11.

Rep. Jerry Nadler (D-N.Y.) and comedian Jon Stewart, a longtime advocate for Sept. 11 families and first responders, joined the mayor at the presser.

“It would be one thing if government had stood alongside survivors and provided them with everything they needed at every step of the way,” Mamdani added, noting that “could not be further” from what occurred.

“People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air,” the mayor continued.

In releasing the records, the Mamdani administration resolved two lawsuits brought by 9/11 Health Watch against New York City.

Ben Chevat, the executive director of the group, thanked Mamdani in a statement “for being the Mayor, after 25 years, who finally begins to answer the question, ‘What did the City know about the dangers from the toxic cloud at Ground Zero and when did it know it?’”

Prior to Mamdani, former mayors Rudy Giuliani (R), Michael Bloomberg (I), Bill de Blasio (D) and Eric Adams (D) led New York City since the attacks. Bloomberg’s party affiliation has changed since he was mayor, but he was in office as a Republican and Independent.

The Sept. 11 attacks killed 2,977 people at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and on board United Airlines Flight 93 that crash landed in Pennsylvania.

The health effects of the attacks have lingered on, as more than 400,000 individuals were exposed to toxic substances as a result of the attacks on the World Trade Center in Manhattan, per the 9/11 Memorial and Museum .

As of December 2024, roughly 140,000 people from all 50 states were enrolled in the World Trade Center (WTC) Health Program, per the memorial. The health program was established under the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act, which former President Obama signed into law in 2011.

The memorial also notes that 49,000 first responders and survivors of the attacks were diagnosed with WTC Health-certified cancers.

When a reporter asked Mamdani about whether Giuliani lied about air quality after Sept. 11, the incumbent mayor said, “I leave it to New Yorkers to make their judgements.”

Mamdani added, “What we want to do is finally allow them the documents that they have long been demanding.”

articles.body:
A House Democrat seeking reelection is selling Zyn-inspired campaign merchandise, leaning into an association with the explosively popular nicotine pouches that have devotees among the Trump administration.

Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) is selling a $50 “ GLUE-ZYN-KAMP ” storage tin on her office campaign website, mimicking the Zyn pouches’ ubiquitous circular container. The Democrat is among the party’s most vulnerable incumbents, running in a district President Trump carried three times.

Zyn’s parent company, Philip Morris International, did not return a request for comment.

Gluesenkamp Perez has crafted a reputation as an independent-minded Democrat, appealing to working class voters. But her race against Washington state Sen. John Braun is a toss-up, with the Republican holding a 2-point edge, according to the Cook Partisan Voting Index.

The GOP considers her seat in Washington’s 3rd Congressional District to be one of its best pickup chances this fall, potentially helping Republicans retain their control of the House.

Zyn pouches contain nicotine but not tobacco. Fans of the pouches say they offer the benefits of nicotine — like alertness and calm — in a discreet package without the known harm of cigarettes.

They have surged in popularity primarily among members of Generation Z, promoted by self-appointed “ Zynfluencers .” But the pouches have also gained a foothold among those in the orbit of Trump’s White House, like Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Former Fox News host Tucker Carlson helped popularize the brand among conservatives before later turning against it and launching his own nicotine pouch product , Alp.

Zyn gained marketing authorization in 2025 when Food and Drug Administration (FDA) officials said the products can help adults cut back on smoking or switch away from cigarettes completely. Nicotine pouches are not FDA-approved, and the agency has said there is no safe tobacco product.

articles.title: Hegseth shakes up the Pentagon as US wages war - but at what cost?
articles.summary: The upheaval in the military could shape the legacy of Trump's second term, writes the BBC's Tom Bateman.
articles.body:
The United States military is at the centre of a fight on two fronts.

First is President Donald Trump's attempt to prise the Strait of Hormuz from Iran's grip; the latest phase of his stalemated war in the Gulf which is drawing in US forces and equipment from around the globe.

The second is a culture war at home in which Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is conducting a promised shake-up at the Pentagon, sparking bitter recriminations and a string of departures including the top civilian in charge of the US Army last week.

The upheaval has triggered questions that could shape the legacy of Trump's second term. Is the US military being stretched to a point that could risk global security? And are these shifts leaving America's extraordinary global network of alliances vulnerable?

Last Monday there was dramatic news from the Pentagon.

One of its most senior political leaders, Dan Driscoll, stepped down as US Secretary of the Army .

Driscoll is not exactly a household name in America, let alone outside it. But his departure mattered. It was the latest twist in a power struggle within the fortress-like walls of the Pentagon over the future of the world's most formidable fighting force.

Driscoll had clashed repeatedly with Hegseth over the nature and speed of military reform. His departure was the latest in a long line of top leaders removed or sidelined by Hegseth.

The level of concern became clear as one Republican Senator Thom Tillis - a frequent Trump critic - called for Hegseth to be fired. "I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country," he said.

"This is not good news. You know, for our nation, for the army," H.R. McMaster, who served as Trump's National Security Adviser during his first term, told CBS when asked about Driscoll's departure. "Secretary Driscoll was pushing… a modernisation agenda to catch the army up."

The backstory of Driscoll's resignation cut deep into issues about the readiness of the US Army. Driscoll wanted urgent modernisation by adding drones throughout ordinary army formations to make it adept for 21st Century warfare.

He said the Ukraine war had shown how the battlefield had changed, with cheap drones and anti-missile systems challenging the US military with its vast bureaucracy and expensive procurement processes.

Hegseth had in fact initiated much of this modernisation plan but subsequently came into conflict with Driscoll, according to reports, as well as with others advocating its rapid expansion.

A source familiar with last week's departure said Driscoll had raised concerns within the administration about army readiness and transformation, which Driscoll said Hegseth was "blocking" specifically by firing the generals responsible.

Jon Duffy, a retired Navy captain and former White House defence policy official, said Driscoll's resignation showed how far Hegseth had "hollowed out" the military leadership at a critical moment.

"You lose the [army] secretary, the chief of staff and other senior leaders driving modernisation, it creates a lot of uncertainty and it disrupts momentum," he said.

"That uncertainty at leadership levels has downstream effects on the force," added Duffy, who had a 30-year career and commanded US warships before joining the White House during the second Obama administration.

In public, Hegseth - a former Army National Guardsman and Fox News pundit - has spent much of his time calling for cultural change to the US military.

He has vowed to end what he called "woke" initiatives and scrap "stupid" rules of engagement he said constrained war fighters' "lethality". He tore up diversity programmes, banned beards and railed against seeing "fat generals in the halls of the Pentagon".

He removed or sidelined the top uniformed officers in charge of the Army, Navy and Air Force as well as at least two dozen generals, admirals and civilian defence leaders, including some of the US military's most decorated officers, often with little explanation.

One critic compares the changes in the top ranks to President Xi Jinping's political purges of the Chinese military which are said to have left serious deficiencies in command structure and readiness.

"We've been conducting a military purge as well, and that has real effects on the ability of our military to be able to discharge its responsibilities," Michael Schiffer, a former top Pentagon official who covered East Asia from 2009 to 2012 under the Obama presidency, told the BBC.

"The way in which [Hegseth is] shaking them up… is bringing on board an awful lot of risk without any apparent way to be able to address or ameliorate it," said Schiffer, who is now a senior fellow at the liberal think-tank the Center for American Progress.

Asked last week about Driscoll's departure, Vice-President JD Vance defended Hegseth, saying he was in "strident agreement" about the need for a culture shift after what he called 40 years of lost wars and "military misadventures".

"What Pete came in wanting to do was revive the warrior spirit in the United States of America," Vance said.

US army secretary resigns after months of tension

US Navy chief leaving post 'effective immediately', Pentagon says

What we should make of CIA boss's secret trip to Moscow

Hegseth attacks Europe over migration with beach 'invasion' D-Day speech

In a statement, the White House told the BBC that President Trump had "full confidence in Secretary Hegseth and the entire Department of War whose record of success in Operation Epic Fury, Operation Absolute Resolve, and Operation Midnight Hammer speaks for itself".

Trump has continued to back Hegseth, standing by him during controversies such as Signalgate and describing him in a phone interview with NBC News last month as "actually one of my best".

Ezra Cohen, a former Under Secretary of Defence during the first Trump administration, described Hegseth's reforms as "bringing in fresh thinking and a more forward-leaning attitude".

But the reported friction among the military leadership and the stalemate with Iran has raised questions about the future of the US military at a critical moment.

Trump's order to launch strikes on Iran on 28 February led to a significant global redistribution of US military resources over the subsequent months. US weapons stored in Europe and Asia were transferred from those regions to replenish supplies in the Gulf.

Europe is now feeling significant "blowback", according to Professor Liana Fix, a Germany-based expert at the Council on Foreign Relations.

She said the lack of communication by the Trump administration with its Nato and European allies ahead of the attack on Iran left relations reeling and accelerated a strategic decision already in process to shift some US military resources away from Europe, particularly as Trump complained that his European allies weren't helping.

Prof Fix said in that context Russian President Vladimir Putin had escalated so-called "hybrid" attacks involving armed drones or sabotage attacks on Nato countries like Germany. Russia denies carrying out the attacks.

"What [Putin] is seeing is not a united stance from the United States and the Europeans to further increase pressure on Russia… he sees that they are weakening, that there are windows and openings of vulnerabilities in Europe," she told the BBC.

Last month, CIA Director John Ratcliffe paid a highly unusual visit to Moscow . He is reported to have delivered a warning to the Kremlin not to test Nato's resolve. But at the same time, one of Hegseth's top officials at the Pentagon, Elbridge Colby, was in Europe to push countries to spend more on their own defence.

Washington had announced a cut of 5,000 from a total 40,000 US troops based in Germany, while a Biden-era plan to deploy a US battalion with long-range Tomahawk missiles to the country was being dropped.

The drawdowns in Europe fit the Trump administration's strategy that predates the Iran war. It sees the Pacific region and Washington's rivalry with China as America's number one national security challenge.

But while the fallout from the Iran war has exacerbated Trump's irritation with Europe and accelerated some US military moves away from the region, it has not been to the immediate benefit of the US presence in the Pacific.

In fact, Washington has also pulled resources from there. Carrier forces were diverted from the Pacific to the Gulf, including the USS Abraham Lincoln and later the Japan-based USS George Washington.

The war is widely assessed to have left critical stocks of American ammunition badly depleted. The US fired about a third of its 3,000-strong stockpile of Tomahawk attack missiles, according to the Washington DC-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).

Its air defence munitions were burned up at an even higher rate, with nearly 1,500 Patriot interceptors - used to shoot down aircraft and cruise and ballistic missiles - fired out of a stockpile of around 2,300, according to the CSIS.

White House Principle Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly said America's "military might" was "stronger than it's ever been".

"The United States Military has more than enough munitions, ammo, and stockpiles to serve all of the Commander-in-Chief's strategic goals and beyond," she said.

Meanwhile Ezra Cohen, the former Trump defence official who is now a fellow at the Hudson Institute, described the president as having degraded Iran's conventional military threat.

Iran's proxy groups are weaker than ever, he said, and in many places they have been completely obliterated, meaning "the president now has additional options and forces in the region to strike other Iranian targets, including nuclear targets, at will".

The strikes might yet take place again. Thousands of troops, including the 82nd Airborne Division, were sent to the Middle East more than six months ago for a deployment that is now stretching into 2027 with no obvious end in sight.

Pictures last week of the USS Abraham Lincoln docking in Thailand with a rusting hull after a gruelling nine months at sea in the Gulf were pounced on by Iran. The regime tried to portray it as a symbol of America's spent efforts.

Hegseth, meanwhile, forcefully rejected claims of abysmal conditions on board. But the narrative war reflected the challenge for Trump and Hegseth as they fight to transform the Pentagon while waging a costly, protracted war.

With additional reporting by Cai Pigliucci

articles.title: Mamdani releases records on toxic air in New York after 9/11 attacks
articles.summary: The New York City mayor said the document release shows victims were ‘lied to’ about health impacts from the attacks.
articles.body:
Just days before the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks, New York City has released a trove of previously undisclosed documents suggesting government efforts to downplay – or even mislead – residents about dangerous air quality following the attacks.

At a news conference on Tuesday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the publication of 170,000 pages concerning health issues following the collapse of two skyscrapers in the World Trade Center complex, known as the Twin Towers.

Mamdani said the effort would deliver “accountability around city government’s response to September 11 that New Yorkers have been denied for years”.

His remarks reinforced long-running suspicions that leaders in the United States prematurely allowed workers and residents back into area around Lower Manhattan where the towers fell.

“It would be one thing if government had stood alongside survivors and provided them with everything they needed at every step of the way. And yet, we know that could not be further from what actually happened,” Mamdani said.

“People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air.”

During the September 11 attacks, the Twin Towers were struck by two hijacked planes, leading to their collapse and the deaths of 2,753 people on site. The destruction sent a cloud of dust across Lower Manhattan. Fires burned in the rubble for months.

Thousands of police officers, firefighters and construction workers spent time working in the soot, often without proper protection.

Within weeks of the collapse, employees and residents were also allowed to return to nearby buildings, including One Liberty Plaza, which had sustained damage during the attacks.

But many of those who worked or lived around the site, known as “Ground Zero”, have seen their health decline in the years since. Some developed respiratory or digestive-system ailments that appeared almost immediately. Others have fallen victim to illnesses that developed over time, including cancer.

Tuesday’s release includes a document sent in October 2001 to then-Deputy Mayor Robert Harding, detailing the city’s potential legal exposure after the 9/11 attacks.

The so-called Harding Memo shows officials anticipated as many as 10,000 lawsuits against the city over issues such as “toxic exposure” due to the poor air quality and “faulty” safety equipment.

The Harding Memo also outlined means through which the city could “limit” its liability, including by appealing to Congress to create a fund for victims and requesting indemnification from the US government.

Another memo, released in February 2002, detailed how officials worried that criticism from US Representative Jerry Nadler could open the city up to “major public relations problems” and a “barrage of lawsuits”.

Ester Fuchs, a former special adviser to then-Mayor Rudy Giuliani, pointed to statements from Nadler accusing the government of quashing documents that “showed higher than acceptable levels of asbestos” in the area around the attack.

Fuchs went on to acknowledge that “there is at least a low level of asbestos in the dust in many buildings in lower Manhattan”. She suggested that, if Nadler’s accusations were correct, the city needed to act.

Asbestos, a mineral used in the construction of the Twin Towers, is also a known carcinogen, linked to scarring of the lungs and mesothelioma, a type of cancer.

“At the least, we should discontinue telling people to clean their apartments with wet mops and rags,” Fuchs wrote, referencing guidance the city had previously released.

Why are the documents being released now?

In the months following the attacks, city and federal officials repeatedly reassured residents, workers and first responders that air-quality levels were safe.

But questions about what – and when – the government knew about air contaminants have persisted in the years after.

The release of Tuesday’s documents addresses a lawsuit brought by advocacy groups like 9/11 Health Watch, which sought to bring to light records about public health after the attacks.

Mamdani highlighted that multi-year legal battle during his remarks on Tuesday, slamming past city governments for failing to act in the public interest.

“Administration after administration has ignored those calling for answers and clarity, instead choosing to bury them in legal arguments and in red tape,” Mamdani said. “We will do no such thing.”

The mayor promised more documents would be shared over the next year, suggesting there could be “millions” of additional pages to come.

Appearing alongside Mamdani were survivors and victims advocates, including comedian Jon Stewart.

Stewart paid tribute to the survivors who fought for government transparency while also battling severe medical conditions.

“I’m not saying that the information may have changed the outcomes, unfortunately, for their families,” Stewart said.

“But I guarantee you it would not have been the struggle that it was to get people to recognise that what they all knew and what we all knew who live in downtown Manhattan: that there was poison in the air and on the ground.”

In a statement, 9/11 Health Watch also praised the records’ release, thanking labour unions, community groups and others for their advocacy work.

“For 25 years, four different Mayoral administrations kept from the public, the U.S. Congress, and the City Council documents showing what the City actually knew about the danger of the toxic chemicals in Lower Manhattan and Western Brooklyn,” Benjamin Chevat, the group’s executive director, said.

He underscored that, even as city officials knew of the dangers, they “continued messaging to the public that the air was ‘safe and acceptable’.”

Nearly 3,000 people died in New York on September 11, 2001, which involved four hijacked planes in total. One hit the Pentagon in Washington, DC, while another crashed into a Pennsylvania field after passengers fought the hijackers.

In the decades since, roughly 4,343 victims have died from illnesses related to the event, according to the World Trade Center Health Program.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates 400,000 people were exposed to toxic contaminants, stressful conditions and situations that put them at risk of physical injury as a result of the attacks.

Mamdani called Tuesday’s document release “the right thing to do”, though it is likely to trigger a wave of new lawsuits against the city for withholding information.

“We hold an obligation each of those New Yorkers to ensure that ‘never forget’ is not just a platitude, but that it is something material,” Mamdani said, citing a common phrase evoked after the 9/11 attack.

Stewart, meanwhile, said the release isn’t just about exposing what the local government knew. It also marks the start of ensuring victims have better access to healthcare moving forward.

“There’s more work to be done,” he said.

articles.title: Carville claims Trump ‘wants to torture’ GOP ahead of midterms
articles.summary: Democratic strategist James Carville speculated Tuesday that President Trump wants his party to lose the midterms. “The only answer that I can come up [with] that explains the current behavior of Donald Trump is simply this: He wants the Republicans to lose. He hates them. He wants to torture them,” Carville told journalist Al Hunt…
articles.body:
Democratic strategist James Carville speculated Tuesday that President Trump wants his party to lose the midterms.

“The only answer that I can come up [with] that explains the current behavior of Donald Trump is simply this: He wants the Republicans to lose. He hates them. He wants to torture them,” Carville told journalist Al Hunt on their “ Politics War Room ” podcast.

“He thinks that he saved them, he taught them how to win, [they] turned [their] back on him and he’s going to teach them a lesson,” the veteran strategist added.

Republicans are trying to keep control of their slim margins in the Senate and House this November, while Democrats are seeking control of Congress for the final two years of Trump’s term.

If the GOP maintains its majorities in both chambers, it will mark the first time the incumbent president’s party has done so since Republicans kept the Senate and House in 2002, during former President George W. Bush’s first term.

Trump has been on the campaign trail in recent weeks, laying out his message to an electorate increasingly dissatisfied with his job performance amid persistent inflation and the Iran war .

“What I want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” the president told attendees of a rally he held alongside Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) last month.

Trump will also speak on both nights of the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas, which starts on Wednesday .

As of Tuesday, Decision Desk HQ gives Democrats a 68 percent chance to retake the House and puts Senate control at 50-50 odds.

Democrats need to flip three seats to take back the lower chamber and four seats to take back the upper chamber. With Vice President Vance as the tiebreaker, Republicans would maintain their majority in Senate in the event of an even split.

During Tuesday’s episode of “Politics War Room,” Carville brought up Trump’s recent dismissal of Americans’ concerns regarding AI as an example of why he wants the GOP to lose the midterms.

“It sounds insane, that you have a president who wants his political party to lose big,” the vocal Trump critic remarked. “But I … can’t think of another explanation … that really answers as many questions as this one does.”

articles.title: US slaps import ban on Canadian alcohol and other goods
articles.summary: It is the latest escalation in a trade war between the two countries, and comes as Canadian retaliatory tariffs on US goods come into force.
articles.body:
The US is banning Canadian products, including alcohol, dairy, and motor vehicles, as Canadian retaliatory tariffs on American goods come into force.

In a series of executive orders on Tuesday, US President Donald Trump wrote that "Canada is discriminating in fact against the commerce of the United States," and ordered the import ban, which will begin 29 September.

Earlier on Tuesday, Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a video address that his country's pivot away from the US as its largest trading partner "will come at a cost".

Both US and Canadian officials have said they would like to strike a deal, but no new talks have been scheduled since negotiations collapsed in late August.

Last month, the White House had imposed 50% tariffs on around $20bn (£14.8bn) of Canadian goods after several rounds of talks had broken down.

Canada responded with dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs on US goods like steel, clothing and furniture. The counter-duties came into effect after midnight on Tuesday.

Tension between the US and Canada has also expanded beyond tariffs.

In August, Trump ordered Lake Ontario to be renamed as Lake America, resulting in uproar from Canadians and some Americans.

articles.title: GOP Gov. Kelly Ayotte and Democrat Cinde Warmington to face off for New Hampshire governorship
articles.summary: New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a Republican, will face off against Democrat Cinde Warmington in November’s general election, NBC News projects, as the incumbent seeks another two-year term.
articles.body: New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a Republican, will face off against Democrat Cinde Warmington in November’s general election, NBC News projects, as the incumbent seeks another two-year term. Ayotte did not face any major challenges in the GOP primary; Warmington ran unopposed in the Democratic primary. New Hampshire is one of two states — Vermont is the other — where a Republican governor is up for re-election after then-Vice President Kamala Harris won the state in 2024. Ayotte, a former state attorney general and U.S. senator, was out of politics for several years between losing re-election in 2016 and winning the governorship in 2024. Warmington served on New Hampshire’s Executive Council, which helps oversee the state budget, from 2021 to 2025. She ran for governor in 2024 and lost in the primary. She has also worked as a health care attorney and in health care management. Warmington is, like many Democrats, focusing her campaign on affordability, while Ayotte is touting accomplishments from her first two years in office. The governor is leading in the early polls and has raised more money, and The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, a nonpartisan election analysis website, rates the race as “leans Republican.”

articles.title: Republican John Sununu and Democrat Chris Pappas win New Hampshire Senate primaries, setting up battleground race
articles.summary: The battleground New Hampshire Senate race is set between Republican former Sen. John Sununu and Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas, NBC News projects, after both prevailed in their primaries Tuesday night.
articles.body: The battleground New Hampshire Senate race is set between Republican former Sen. John Sununu and Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas, NBC News projects, after both prevailed in their primaries Tuesday night. Pappas defeated scientist Karishma Manzur, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, in his primary, leading 62%-36% with about one-fifth of the vote counted. But it appears he could fall short of the support from primary voters that the Pappas campaign touted in recent internal polling. The race could be key to the fight for the Senate majority in November. Republicans are confident that Sununu, a member of a well-known political family, can put the race in play. But Democrats dismiss GOP optimism in a state that President Donald Trump has never won. Trump endorsed Sununu in the primary against former Massachusetts Sen. Scott Brown, who also served as an ambassador during Trump’s first term. Sununu had 70% support to Brown’s 25% with about a sixth of the vote counted. First elected to the House in 2018, Pappas has long been viewed as the frontrunner in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. And Pappas had already started to focus on the likely general election contest against Sununu, launching an attack against Sununu in mid-August. “In Congress, Sununu gave huge tax breaks to pharma companies and sided with the insurance industry, and then he went to work for them and made $35 million,” Pappas said in the ad. “In Washington, I’m taking on this kind of corruption, refusing corporate PAC money and fighting to lower costs.” Republicans, meanwhile, have already begun to attack Pappas. One Nation, the non-profit arm of the GOP super PAC Senate leadership fund, launched an ad knocking Pappas on taxes. The spot alleges the congressman “gave out tax breaks to New Yorkers for their million dollar homes” when he supported a sweeping climate and social safety net measure in 2021. Trump’s approval rating is down and voters are raising concerns about the economy and the Iran war as the midterms approach. But Republicans are still optimistic with Sununu on the ballot in New Hampshire. Sununu’s father and brother both served as governors of the state, and Sununu himself represented New Hampshire in the Senate from 2003 through 2008 after serving in the House. He lost his bid for re-election in 2008 to Shaheen, who then served three terms before retiring this year. Republicans believe they could have an opening with independent voters in the state who are averse to higher taxes, and they have GOP Gov. Kelly Ayotte on the ticket as she runs for a second two-year term. Ayotte is the last Republican to win a Senate race in New Hampshire, winning her first term in 2010 before losing re-election in 2016. But Democrats dismiss Republicans’ optimism about New Hampshire. Lauren French, a spokesperson for the Democratic super PAC Senate Majority PAC, acknowledged in a recent interview the New Hampshire race would be competitive, but said Democrats were confident they would prevail. “New Hampshire feels like wish casting in a lot of ways,” French said of Republican optimism about the state. “We continue to put states that they didn’t even think were going to be competitive on the board, so they need to continue to assure donors, right, that they are also doing the same.”

articles.body:
New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte is projected to face off against Democrat Cinde Warmington as she seeks a second term in the Granite State’s governor’s mansion, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

DDHQ and Cook Political Report forecast Ayotte is “likely” hold on to her post in November.

Ayotte easily clinched the Republican nomination, leading two GOP challengers by nearly 88 percentage points with 17 percent of the vote counted as of 8 p.m. EDT Tuesday, per DDHQ.

Warmington, a former New Hampshire executive councilor, ran unsuccessfully for the Democratic nomination in 2024, losing to former Manchester Mayor Joyce Craig (D). Ayotte beat Craig by nearly 10 percentage points in the general election.

Warmington ran uncontested for the Democratic nomination this time around, notching support from New Hampshire Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (D) and Maggie Hassan (D).

Recent polls show Ayotte leading Warmington by about 10 points in the general election.

Pappas defeated four other Democrats for the party nod, with his most serious challenger being scientist Karishma Manzur. Meanwhile, Sununu beat…
articles.body:
Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) and former Sen. John E. Sununu (R-N.H.) are projected to face off against each other for retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s (D-N.H.) seat in the Granite State, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Pappas defeated four other Democrats for the party nod, with his most serious challenger being scientist Karishma Manzur. Meanwhile, Sununu beat former Sen. Scott Brown (R-Mass.), who was among seven other Republicans vying for the GOP bid.

Pappas led Manzur by about 22 percentage points with 22 percent of the vote reported, while Sununu defeated Brown by about 35 points with 17 percent of the vote counted by DDHQ as of 8 p.m. EDT Tuesday.

Pappas and Sununu were long considered the party frontrunners for the seat.

New Hampshire represents one of Republicans’ best pickup opportunities this fall, with the GOP scoring a win in courting John E. Sununu to run for his old job. Shaheen unseated the elder Sununu, who served between the House and Senate from 1997 to 2009, during his 2008 reelection bid.

The elder Sununu decided to launch a Senate campaign after former Gov. Chris Sununu (R), his brother, opted against running.

The Granite State, part of the lineup of early presidential primary states, hasn’t elected a Republican for Senate since 2010, when Gov. Kelly Ayotte (R) won a term in the upper chamber. She was later defeated in 2016 by Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.).

Still, New Hampshire is viewed as a competitive state and has shown a willingness to ticket-split. Ayotte won her gubernatorial race in 2024 while the state also elected Pappas and Rep. Maggie Goodlander (D-N.H.).

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rates Shaheen’s seat “lean Democrat.”

articles.title: Trump’s pick wins GOP primary for open Pappas House seat
articles.summary: Anthony DiLorenzo, President Trump’s pick for an open House seat in New Hampshire, is projected to win the Republican nomination, according to Decision Desk HQ. DiLorenzo defeated Hollie Noveletsky, a military veteran and businesswoman, to advance to the general election in what will likely be a pivotal race for control of the House. His primary…
articles.body:
Anthony DiLorenzo, President Trump’s pick for an open House seat in New Hampshire, is projected to win the Republican nomination, according to Decision Desk HQ.

DiLorenzo defeated Hollie Noveletsky, a military veteran and businesswoman, to advance to the general election in what will likely be a pivotal race for control of the House. His primary marks a a victory for the president, who has had a mixed track record with his endorsements this primary season.

President Trump endorsed DiLorenzo, an auto businessman who started a chain of car dealerships and collision centers, in July, writing on Truth Social, “As a very successful Businessman and Entrepreneur, Anthony understands the America First Policies required to Create GREAT Jobs, Cut Taxes and Regulations, Unleash American Energy DOMINANCE, Promote MADE IN THE U.S.A., and Champion our Nation’s Golden Age.”

Noveletsky, who runs her family’s iron works business, is also highly supportive of the president’s agenda, including hot-button issues such as immigration and tariffs. When President Trump endorsed her opponent, she called his decision “wrong” and committed to staying in the race.

Since the endorsement, DiLorenzo has sought to moderately distance himself from President Trump, telling WMUR, “When I’m in agreement with the president, I’m happy to do so, if it benefits the people in New Hampshire.”

“And if I disagree with the president, I would let him know — and not on national TV, in a private setting, just like he did to me when he called me up and said, ‘I’m going to endorse you,'” he added.

New Hampshire’s 1st District has been in Democratic hands for 16 of the past 20 years, held by former Rep. Carol Shea-Porter (D-N.H.) and then Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.), the incumbent who opted to run for the open Senate seat in the Granite State instead of seeking reelection. Republican former Rep. Pete Guinta held the seat for two non-consecutive terms in the 2010s.

Pappas, who is seeking to replace retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, defeated his Republican opponent for the House seat by over eight percent in 2024, while Kamala Harris only won the state by just under two points.

DiLorenzo will likely face either Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of Jeanee Shaheen, or Maura Sullivan, a former Marine, in November.

articles.title: Ex-GOP senator clears hurdle in crucial comeback bid as Republicans try to flip key Senate seat
articles.summary: John E. Sununu defeated Scott Brown for the GOP Senate nomination in New Hampshire, a key race that could determine Republican majority control.
articles.body: Former Sen. John E. Sununu on Tuesday won the GOP Senate nomination in swing state New Hampshire, in a race that may determine if Republicans keep control of the chamber in the midterm elections. Sununu defeated former Sen. Scott Brown, the Associated Press reports, in the showdown to succeed retiring longtime Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the first woman in the nation's history elected governor and senator. Republicans haven't won a Senate election in New Hampshire in 16 years, but they view the open Democrat-held seat as a top flip opportunity in the fight to hold their slim majority in the midterms. Sununu will now face off in the general election against either four-term Rep. Chris Pappas or socialist candidate and scientist Karishma Manzur, who are battling for the Democratic nomination. THESE 12 MIDTERM RACES WILL DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE SENATE Sununu, the son of former Gov. John H. Sununu and older brother to former Gov. Chris Sununu, is a former congressman and senator who is aiming to return to the Senate. President Donald Trump in February endorsed Sununu, a longtime GOP Trump critic, over Brown, one of Trump's first-term ambassadors. Sununu was also backed by Senate Majority Leader John Thune and the National Republican Senatorial Committee. Brown charged in a Fox News Digital interview that Sununu's "got 70 endorsements on his website, but he doesn't have the president’s. He never talks about it. He's embarrassed by it." "I've had the MAGA base and a lot of those so-called traditional Republicans for almost over a year," Brown highlighted. "Johnny came lately, and he's here, and now he thinks everyone's going to just vote for him. That's not how it works. You got to go earn it." DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Brown claimed that Sununu is "beholden" to Trump, Thune, the Senate leadership, and outside groups. "He owes them everything. He doesn't work for the people of New Hampshire," Brown charged. But Sununu told Fox News Digital, "I'll have one job stand up for the people of New Hampshire every single day... I don't need to make anyone in Washington happy. It's all about our state, our communities, our economy, and our small businesses." Asked by about Trump's endorsement, Sununu didn't mention the president's name but highlighted his local endorsements, saying "we've received tremendous support in New Hampshire... we've got great momentum at the grassroots level." Trump last week said he'd be heading out on the campaign trail to help fellow Republicans running in the midterms. Asked if he'd like Trump to join him on the Granite State campaign trail, Sununu answered, "I don't need anyone from outside New Hampshire to campaign for me. I've said that from the very beginning." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The former senator also disagreed with the Trump administration's trade war with neighboring Canada, saying "I don't think it's the right thing to pick a trade war with Canada. They're a great trading partner for New Hampshire." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Republicans are facing a rough political climate heading into the midterms, due persistent inflation, high gas prices fueled by what polls indicate is an unpopular war with Iran, and Trump's underwater approval ratings. But Sununu, who defeated Shaheen in 2002 to win election to the Senate but lost a rematch to her six years later, said he's "focused on the right things, affordability, bringing down the cost of living on housing, health care, and energy, a reform agenda."
